prompt: ipcalc printed `Hosts/Net: 62` for 10.20.32.0/26. How many usable host addresses does any /26 hold?
hint: Every /26 is the same size.

prompt: With a /26 for every network, the link between r1 and r2 uses 2 of its host addresses. How many host addresses of that subnet go unused?
hint: A /26 has 62 host addresses.

prompt: To fit sales, every network gets a /25 instead. How many addresses do the four /25s take in total?
hint: A /25 is 128 addresses.

prompt: Why does cutting 10.20.32.0/24 into four equal /26s fail this company?
hint: Compare 62 with each need.

choices.text: Sales needs 100, and a /26 holds 62
choices.why: Right. However the four are arranged, the largest network does not fit.

choices.text: A /24 has no room for four subnets of any size
choices.why: It has: four /26s, as ipcalc measured.

choices.text: The link needs over 62
choices.why: The link needs 2; it is where the waste is, not the shortage.

choices.text: Four /26s add up to more than 256 addresses
choices.why: They add up to exactly 256.

prompt: Giving every subnet a mask that fits its own size goes by a four-letter abbreviation: ___.
hint: The V stands for variable.

prompt: Put the steps of a VLSM plan in order.
hint: The sizes must be known before anything is placed.
items: List the networks and the hosts each needs
Add two to each and round up to a power of two
Give each one the next free address
trap: Placing before sorting is the usual slip: a small subnet placed first can sit where a big one needed to start.

prompt: A network needs 20 hosts. What prefix length does the plan give it? Answer with the number after the slash.
hint: 20 plus 2, rounded up to a power of two.

prompt: A network needs 60 hosts. What prefix length does it get? Answer with the number after the slash.
hint: Add the two addresses nobody can use first.

prompt: A network needs 63 hosts. What prefix length does it get? Answer with the number after the slash.
hint: 63 plus 2 is more than 64.

prompt: ipcalc said `Needed size: 228 addresses` for a plan inside 10.20.32.0/24. How many addresses of the /24 are left unused?
hint: A /24 is 256 addresses.

prompt: Somebody first places the link at 10.20.32.64/30 and operations at 10.20.32.192/27. 220 addresses are still free. Why can sales' /25 no longer be placed?
hint: Where may a /25 start?

choices.text: Both places a /25 may start are taken
choices.why: Right. Free space is not enough; it has to be an aligned block of 128.

choices.text: A /25 needs 256 free addresses, and 220 is less
choices.why: A /25 is 128 addresses; 220 would be plenty if they were in one piece.

choices.text: The link has to be the last subnet placed in the block
choices.why: The link can sit anywhere aligned to 4; the trouble is where it sits now.

choices.text: ipcalc refuses to place subnets out of order
choices.why: This was placed by hand; no tool was asked.

prompt: Match each need of this lesson's plan to the prefix it gets.
hint: Add two, round up to a power of two.

prompt: r1's table holds `10.20.32.128/26 dev eth2 proto kernel scope link`, and nobody typed that route. Where did it come from?
hint: What was typed on eth2?

choices.text: r2 announced it to r1 over the link between them
choices.why: r2 holds one /24 and announces nothing; there is no routing protocol here.

choices.text: From the address 10.20.32.129/26 set on eth2
choices.why: Right. An address with a mask says which network is on that cable, and the kernel adds the route.

choices.text: From the default route
choices.why: The default points at r2, not at eth2.

choices.text: ipcalc wrote it
choices.why: ipcalc calculates; it configures nothing.

prompt: How many routes does r2's table use to reach sales, engineering and operations together?
hint: Read r2's `ip route`.

prompt: hq1's traceroute to ops1 lists 10.20.99.1, then 10.20.32.225, then 10.20.32.200. Which machine answered as 10.20.32.225?
hint: Look at the /30 in the plan.

choices.text: r2, answering from its head-office side
choices.why: That is the first hop, 10.20.99.1.

choices.text: r1, at its end of the link to r2
choices.why: Right. r1 holds .225 and r2 holds .226 on the /30.

choices.text: ops1's gateway, on r1's eth3
choices.why: That address is 10.20.32.193.

choices.text: r2, at its own end of the /30
choices.why: r2's end of the /30 is .226.

prompt: Which addresses are the default gateways of the three LANs in this plan? Choose all that apply.
hint: The first host address of each subnet.

choices.why: Right: sales' gateway, on r1's eth1.
Right: engineering's, on eth2.
Right: operations', on eth3.
That is r1's end of the link to r2, not a LAN's gateway.
That is engineering's network address; no host can use it.

prompt: r2 holds `10.20.32.0/24 via 10.20.32.225`. What does r2 do with a packet for 10.20.32.250, an address nobody has?
hint: Ask r2's table, not the plan.

choices.text: Drops it, because no subnet of the plan holds it
choices.why: r2 does not know the subnets; it knows the /24.

choices.text: Sends it to r1, like any address in the /24
choices.why: Right: `ip route get` gave the same answer for .250 as for .140.

choices.text: Answers hq1 with Destination Host Unreachable
choices.why: That came later, from r1, once r1 had a route that refuses.

choices.text: Returns it to hq1
choices.why: A router forwards by its table; it does not send packets back to their source.

prompt: Why did the ping to 10.20.32.250 come back as `Time to live exceeded` from 10.20.32.225?
hint: What does r1 do with an address it has no subnet for?

choices.text: r1 had no route for it and dropped it on arrival
choices.why: A drop would print nothing, or Unreachable; this one went round.

choices.text: ops1 was too far away for a TTL of 64
choices.why: ops1 answered at three hops in the same lab.

choices.text: r1 sent it back to r2 by its default, and round it went until the TTL ran out
choices.why: Right. The traceroute shows .225, .226, .225: r1, r2, r1.

choices.text: hq1 set a TTL of 1 on its ping
choices.why: A normal ping starts at 64; the TTL was spent going round.

prompt: On r1, the route that stopped the loop was typed as `ip route add ___ 10.20.32.0/24`.
hint: Its answer to every packet is "no".

prompt: Summarise 10.20.32.192/27 and 10.20.32.224/27 into one route. What is its prefix length? Answer with the number after the slash.
hint: Count the bits the two have in common.

prompt: After `ip route add unreachable 10.20.32.0/24` on r1, why does a ping to 10.20.32.140 still get its answer?
hint: Two of r1's routes contain .140.

choices.text: The unreachable route applies to pings from hq1 alone
choices.why: A route applies to every packet for its prefix.

choices.text: The /26 for eng is longer, so it wins
choices.why: Right. The /24 only answers for what nothing more specific holds.

choices.text: r2 sends .140 to r1 by a different path
choices.why: r2 has one route for the whole /24.

choices.text: The kernel ignores a route typed after the others
choices.why: Order does not matter; length does.

prompt: After 10.20.32.130/25 was added on eth3, `ip route get 10.20.32.180` still says `dev eth2`. Why?
hint: Which of the two routes is longer?

choices.text: The /26 is longer than the /25
choices.why: Right: .180 is inside both, and the longest prefix decides.

choices.text: The new address had not taken effect yet
choices.why: The /25 was already in the table, listed by `ip route`.

choices.text: eth3 was down at the time
choices.why: Nothing in the capture brings eth3 down; ops1 is still on it.

choices.text: .180 lies outside the new /25 altogether
choices.why: The /25 runs from .128 to .255, so .180 is inside it.

prompt: How many addresses do 10.20.32.128/25 and engineering's 10.20.32.128/26 have in common?
hint: One of them contains the other.

prompt: Which of the plan's subnets lie inside the mistaken 10.20.32.128/25? Choose all that apply.
hint: The /25 runs from .128 to .255.

choices.text: Engineering's 10.20.32.128/26
choices.why: Right, .128 to .191.
Right, .192 to .223.
Right, .224 to .227.
Sales is the other half, .0 to .127.

choices.text: Head office's 10.20.99.0/24
choices.why: That is a different block altogether.

prompt: Two CIDR blocks overlap. Which of these is then true of them?
hint: A block starts at a multiple of its own size.

choices.text: They share a few addresses at one edge
choices.why: Aligned blocks cannot meet halfway like that.

choices.text: They have the same prefix length
choices.why: Two equal-length blocks that overlap are the same block.

choices.text: One of them contains the other
choices.why: Right. Aligned blocks nest or do not touch.

choices.text: Their network addresses differ by one
choices.why: Nothing about overlap depends on that.

prompt: Plan subnets for 30, 12 and 5 hosts, largest first, starting at 10.20.40.0. At what address does the third one start? Give its last number.
hint: A /27, then a /28, then a /29.

prompt: Match each prefix to the usable hosts it holds.
hint: Two to the power of the host bits, minus two.

prompt: The plan's free space is 10.20.32.228/30, .232/29 and .240/28. A new team needs 12 hosts. Which subnet does it get?
hint: 12 plus 2, rounded up, and it must start on a multiple of its size.

choices.why: .228 is not a multiple of 16, so a /28 cannot start there.
Right: 16 addresses, 14 hosts, aligned, and free.
A /28 from .232 is not aligned and would take part of .240/28 with it.
That block holds the r1–r2 link.
